title: Why the Army Bet on Camels
topic: Why the U.S. Army used camels in the Southwest desert in the 1850s (to improve logistics in arid terrain)

lines: A Secretary of War begged Congress for camels.
Jefferson Davis wanted them to haul supplies across the desert Southwest.
Soldiers stared at the humped beasts arriving from the Mediterranean.
Mules were the Army way.
Camels? Nobody knew how to handle them.
Major Wayne shipped 34 camels to Texas in 1856.
A second voyage brought 41 more.
The herd reached 70.
In 1857, Edward Beale led 25 camels on a wagon road survey.
Each camel carried 600 pounds.
Beale said one camel beat four mules.
You see, a mule needs water and rest.
Camels drink once, then keep walking for days.
In 1859, Lieutenant Hartz marched camels 85 miles with no water.
They showed no thirst.
Horses and mules arrived distressed; camels did not.
The Army still said no.
Then the Civil War hit.
Camels were sold at auction in 1864.
The last one was seen in Arizona in 1891.

claims.claim: Jefferson Davis, as Secretary of War, pushed for camels to improve Army transportation in the southwestern US.
Major Wayne procured camels; 34 arrived at Indianola, Texas on May 14, 1856; a second voyage brought 41 more, giving the Army 70 camels.
In 1857, Edward Beale led an expedition with 25 pack camels; each camel carried 600 pounds; Beale said he would rather have one camel than four mules.
In 1859, Lieutenant Hartz led a camel expedition that traveled about 85 miles without watering the camels; the camels showed no desire for water; horses and mules were distressed but camels were not.
The Army abandoned the camel experiment; camels were sold at auction in 1864; the last animal from California was reportedly seen in Arizona in 1891.
